etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French citer, from Latin citare (“to cause to move, excite, summon”), frequentative of ciēre (“to rouse, excite, call”). Sense 4 is the original one.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To quote; to repeat, as a passage from a book, or the words of another.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, Gary Younge, “Hypocrisy lies at heart of Manning prosecution”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 18:
quote.text: WikiLeaks did not cause these uprisings but it certainly informed them. The dispatches revealed details of corruption and kleptocracy that many Tunisians suspected, but could not prove, and would cite as they took to the streets.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To mention; to make mention of.

quote.citation: 2023 June 30, Marina Hyde, “The tide is coming in fast on Rishi Sunak – and it’s full of sewage”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: Until then, the Sunak administration remains a study in ineffectuality on multiple fronts, leading Goldsmith to cite, not unreasonably, “a kind of paralysis”.

definitions.definition: To list the source(s) from which one took information, words or literary or verbal context.
(transitive, law) To summon officially or authoritatively to appear in court.

quote.citation: 2023 August 29, “Tribal ranger draws weapon on climate activists blocking road to Burning Man; conduct under review”, in AP News‎[2]:
quote.text: According to the tribe’s chairman, rangers cited five of the demonstrators, who had traveled to Nevada from New York, Washington, California and the European country of Malta. The chairman did not say what they were cited for.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the first syllable of citation. Analogous to quote, from quotation.
